subtopic: PROPOSAL TO MAINTAIN DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME TO CONSERVE ENERGY

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP FAIR AND JUST POLICIES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS RESOURCES
speechtext:
That this House regrets the failure of the government to develop and apply policies in the fields of the oil and gas non-renewable energy resources that are fair or just or adequate for the people or the provinces of Canada today or for the future.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable regret that I have to be critical of the government again today, having had to be critical of it last night; but one has to be truthful when speaking in this chamber and the subject matter of this motion will fit in with what I was saying last night. Hon. gentlemen opposite came into office on the basis of co-operative federalism, but they have now degenerated to strong-arm federalism or, as I said last night, to forced federalism or goon-squad federalism-anything but co-operative federalism. They came into office on the basis of participatory democracy, which has also vanished into limbo because the only democracy now is conference-hall autocracy.
The same thing is true in the energy field. What is the good of hon. gentlemen opposite publishing the study called "An Energy Strategy for Canada" when they ignore the recommendations of their own study or twist it in their administration so that it is unfair and unjust, as this motion says. The motion says that their policies are neither fair, just nor adequate for the people or the provinces of Canada.
1 want to touch on three subjects in the short time allotted to me which I believe is 30 minutes. First, I want to touch on the new conservation policy, announced by the minister at the beginning of February, for Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island dealing allegedly with conservation of energy in those two provinces and confining it to those two provinces for spurious reasons. Second, I want to touch on the failure of the

February 23, 1977
Energy Policy
government to adopt a fair and just policy with regard to offshore minerals, the minerals off the shores of British Columbia, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Quebec and Newfoundland.
Third, I want to touch on the failure of the government to do anything in the field of hydro development or in the field of financing or assisting hydro development, particularly with reference to the possible development in Labrador of hydro resources there; the government's picayune, penny-pinching policy with respect to those resources; and its failure to assist Newfoundland, for example, in developing the Gull Island project, one which would produce enough hydro energy to replace imports of 18 million barrels of oil a year.
With regard to the new policy announced by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) at the beginning of February, the federal government announced assistance to Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. The minister announced a policy which would assist householders primarily in the provinces of P.E.I. and Nova Scotia in January and February. In the case of P.E.I., the program amounted to $12 million, of which $6.94 million was for a new home insulation program to be administered by CMHC. There are some other programs with regard to energy conservation and studits, but the main program is to help householders insulate their homes to save energy costs. This is a program of grants to householders in P.E.I. Prince Edward Island was selected and isolated for this treatment, together with Nova Scotia, because of its extremely high reliance on costly imported oil for electrical power generation.
The reason given for discriminating against the other eight provinces of Canada and- restricting this program to Nova Scotia and P.E.I. was the costly imported oil for electrical power generation. In Nova Scotia and P.E.I., under this program people can get a grant of $350 if they want to insulate their homes themselves. They can get a grant of up to $500 if they have the work done by contractors. If you are a householder in Newfoundland, the Northwest Territories, Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba or Alberta, you will receive no assistance from the government except possibly a loan program from CMHC.
The reason given for this discrimination is that Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island rely heavily on oil for electrical generation. It is true that they do. As a matter of fact, according to the release issued by the minister, Prince Edward Island has a 100 per cent dependence on oil for electrical generation, and Nova Scotia 63 per cent. In making that point the minister's officials have gone on in a statement to give a misleading figure for Newfoundland, In appendix C to this release they say of Prince Edward Island-and the same in the release for Nova Scotia-that Newfoundland's dependence on oil for electrical generation is 1.2 per cent. That is to make Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, which are being treated differently, look more plausible. What appendix C does not state is that they include in the Newfoundland figure all of Newfoundland and Labrador, including the huge hydro

project at Churchill Falls which delivers nearly all the 5,600 megawatts to Quebec. That is ail put into the Newfoundland figure to show that our dependency on oil is just 1.2 per cent.
That is a false and misleading figure. As a matter of fact, Newfoundland's dependency on oil for electrical generation in 1975 was 8 per cent on the island of Newfoundland where the bulk of the population lives-about half a million of them. In the present year it is going to be in the order of 21 per cent because the island of Newfoundland no longer has any hydro resources to develop and is left with the only alternative, oil-fired steam. So the releases put out by the federal government are not true or factual. They are designed to mislead. They are neither fair nor just. It is not 1.2 per cent in Newfoundland; in 1977 it will be 21 per cent on the island of Newfoundland.
Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, these two provinces are highly dependent on oil for generating electricity. But what has this to do with the new policy of helping the householder? The minister's own release shows, for Nova Scotia, that the percentage of households using oil heating, not electrical heating, is 90 per cent. That is shown in appendix E. In connection with both Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, the release shows the dependency of Prince Edward Island householders for heating purposes is 100 per cent oil. In other words, in Nova Scotia 90 per cent of all households are heated using oil, oil furnaces or oil stoves, and in Prince Edward Island it is 100 per cent.
How does this policy of giving a householder a grant of $500 to insulate his home to save energy costs have anything to do with electricity? How does it save the use of oil for electricity in Nova Scotia? It has no connection with electricity. If 100 per cent of the homes in Prince Edward Island were electrically heated, and 90 per cent of the homes in Nova Scotia were electrically heated, and the electricity came from oil, one would be saving electricity and the oil used to generate it. That is not the case when it is going to go to households heated by furnaces that use oif directly.
If the object of this policy is to conserve oil and to conserve the imports of oil in addition to saving people money, then is a barrel of oil saved in Newfoundland or in Ontario not just as good to Canada as a barrel saved in Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island? Do the people of Canada realize they are being discriminated against in this way? Just because of geographical location in two of the ten provinces of Canada the householders can get a substantial cash advance to insulate their homes. The minister's statements say that if they do this properly they will save 40 per cent of their energy requirements-40 per cent of the cost of heating their homes. You can get that in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, but you cannot get it in the other eight provinces.
This is pure discrimination, Mr. Speaker. The government is using the excuse that there is more oil-fired electricity in those two provinces, but that does not carry any weight. It is not the real reason. This is going to be a $12 million program in Prince Edward Island and $80 million in Nova Scotia, of which $17 million is to come from the government of Nova
February 23, 1977

Scotia. In Nova Scotia it is $33.41 million for the home insulation grant program and another $17 million for a home insulation loan program, and almost $7 million in Prince Edward Island.
What is the reason for this discrimination? It has nothing to do with the reason given in the statement. It has been stated publicly that Nova Scotia is the author of its own misfortunes with respect to high energy costs. The government of Nova Scotia turned down the opportunity to go into nuclear energy with New Brunswick. Because the government of Nova Scotia prevented increases in prices charged for electricity over the last three or four years-Premier Regan prevented them from going ahead when they should have commenced earlier-now there is going to be an abrupt jump. For political reasons they were kept down over three or four years when costs were climbing. The Nova Scotia Power Commission incurred heavy losses because of that political policy. That is the reason they are taking an abrupt jump in Nova Scotia now. It is because they had the benefit of an Imperial Oil contract to supply oil for electrical generation purposes at a very low figure. Now there has to be an abrupt jump. There have been abrupt jumps in Newfoundland and all the other provinces, Mr. Speaker.
The person who put forward these reasons for not giving Nova Scotia special help was the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources last year. He has been made to swallow his words by some forces beyond his control. What were those forces? They were political forces. The Liberal party of Nova Scotia got the government House leader down to Nova Scotia and pulverized him at a meeting about six months ago. They assured the minister that he had no chance of being elected and would have to go to the other place if he did not get a special program from the government of Canada. For six months Nova Scotia was rife with Alastair Gillespie jokes. It was not the Newfie joke in Nova Scotia; it was the Alastair Gillespie joke. The hon. gentleman has made a 100 per cent about-face in the face of this abuse.

speechtext: He is still facing in the wrong direction.

speechtext:
After the abuse he took from the government of Nova Scotia, he brought in this new policy. There are two Liberal provinces left in Canada, Mr. Speaker, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, and the federal government is struggling mightily to see that they remain Liberal. Nova Scotia faces an election this year. This about-face reminds me of the following ditty.
When Regan delved and MacEachen spanned Who was then in command?
Certainly not the energy man.
I am sure the minister fought against this policy in the confines of the government, but he has been forced to toe the line by the government House leader and Premier Regan. This is a sad thing because the people of the other eight provinces are being discriminated against by the government. It is using tax moneys collected all across Canada to support a policy that discriminates against the other eight provinces, for no logical
Energy Policy
reason-nothing but a political reason. That is why this resolution decries the unfairness and injustice of these policies.
I have not the time to go into more detail about how silly it is to argue that only these two provinces deserve this policy because of their high content of oil-fired energy, 100 per cent in Prince Edward Island and 60 per cent in Nova Scotia. 1 support this kind of program in an attempt to induce energy conservation. It would be a step in the right direction were it applied all across Canada. But I say that what is good for Nova Scotia and what is good for Prince Edward Island is good for the rest of us Canadians.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: You sound like General Motors.

speechtext:
The province of Newfoundland has been attempting to get equal treatment with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick since March, 1976, including letters from the premier of the province outlining reasons why we should receive at least the same treatment. I will briefly give some of these reasons; they would apply to other provinces as well. The people of Newfoundland are depending increasingly on imported oil to meet their energy needs-21 per cent this year. If hon. members opposite do not adopt a proper policy in developing hydro energy or to assist provinces with low capability to develop hydro resources, it will be ever-increasing: it will be 40 per cent in 1980.
We need assistance for that reason. We need assistance because the per capita personal income in Newfoundland is lower than in Nova Scotia, and about the same as in Prince Edward Island. If you look at need, you cannot just take one item such as the high electricity cost and isolate that. You have to look at all of the factors. The cost of living in Newfoundland is the highest in the country. You have to look at other factors like that to get that need. When you look at those factors you see that the need of Newfoundlanders is even greater than those in Nova Scotia and is equal to those in Prince Edward Island. It is also true for other parts of the country. Our climate has higher average temperatures than Prince Edward Island or Nova Scotia. We have higher wind velocities than P.E.I. or Nova Scotia.

speechtext: That is true.

speechtext:
I am not trying to illustrate that fact today. The cost of heating oil in Newfoundland is substantially higher than in Nova Scotia. It costs 3'A cents more for a gallon of heating oil in St. John's than it does in Halifax. The same is true of stove oil. The cost of heating oil is greater in Newfoundland than in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Seventy per cent of our households are heated by stove oil furnaces. Therefore, the need is greater there. Our electricity prices are the third highest in Canada despite the fact that we have a lot of hydro. It is high-cost hydro because it was only developed in the last 15 years at a high capital cost. It is delivered to scattered outposts. In addition, we have a rural

I could go on with a number of other reasons which show that Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island should not be singled out from the other provinces with respect to all these needs. By 1980, 40 per cent of the people of Newfoundland will be depending on oil-fired steam power. We cannot use coal and we cannot use nuclear: we have only one alternative to our hydro power in Newfoundland, and that is oil. We will hear the minister attempt, if he can, to justify this discrimination when he speaks. I say to the people of the other eight provinces that it is time they woke up and put some pressure on this government to start treating them fairly and start offering them the same energy conservation grants that householders in Nova Scotia and P.E.I. have been offered, as well as those in the Northwest Territories. This is not an energy conservation policy. This is a policy of political poltroonery, political preference. It is the rankest kind of discrimination.
I do not know the population figures, but at least 90 per cent of the people of Canada should be getting this. They should all be able to reduce the energy consumption in their homes across the country. 1 will be interested in hearing how the minister is going to continue to support this as a policy for those two provinces without extending it to the rest of us across this country who are so badly in need. As a matter of fact, unless he does change that policy I will try, as I said last night, to get his salary reduced to two cents when the estimates come before the House.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
His energy strategy reads well until one looks to see how it is being carried out. It then becomes intermingled with the rankest kind of political consideration.
I now come to the second reason for moving this motion that the government's policies are unfair and unjust to the rest of the people of Canada. There are a dozen reasons and these will be discussed by other speakers. I shall only touch on two or three. I refer to the government's offshore minerals policy. The Liberal government in Ottawa argues that it owns and must control offshore mineral rights off the west and east coasts of Canada, our reserves of oil and gas. The Northwest Territories are not enough for them, the territories they already own; they want to own the resources that lie off both coasts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP FAIR AND JUST POLICIES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS RESOURCES
speechtext: All three coasts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP FAIR AND JUST POLICIES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS RESOURCES
speechtext:
However many coasts. They already have the Northwest Territories. In 1967 they got an opinion from the Supreme Court of Canada that in fact the federal government owns the continental shelf and controls and owns all the minerals that might lie off British Columbia. They got this through a narrow legalistic interpretation of the constitution. Because of that they are now attempting to claim that they own and must control the minerals that lie off the east coast as well. Why? What is the difference between minerals that lie under the land in Manitoba and Saskatchewan and minerals

that are under the water off Newfoundland, Nova Scotia or British Columbia? Why, because they are under the water, should they belong to the government of Canada? If some court, through narrow legalistic reasoning, finds that the federal government has technical ownership, why should that government insist upon it? It would only insist upon if it was a centralizing government, a government that does not believe in federalism, a government that does not care whether the provinces stand or fall.
Does this government want the provinces to remain weak financially and subservient to the central power? The government has aggravated and irritated provinces such as Alberta and Saskatchewan because they want to use their own resources for their own benefit and get as much as they can out of it. It is the kind of government which claims it owns them and therefore is going to control them. That is the attitude of the hon. gentlemen opposite.
The federal government has entered into agreement with the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. At the beginning of February they made public an abbreviated version of the agreement reached with those three provinces. They have no agreement with Newfoundland or Quebec because we do not ever intend to agree with the Liberal policy in this direction. However, they have secured agreement with these three provinces which are not as strong as Newfoundland.
We were treated to a fantastic exhibition. Premier Regan almost laughed himself silly because he was so happy about this agreement. Why would he go along with such a piece of play-acting, because it is a pernicious agreement, an agreement that leaves all control with the government of Canada. It does not help those provinces fundamentally at all. The agreement gives away the control over oil and gas and the regulation of what the royalty system is going to be: all that is left with the government of Canada. The provinces are told they can have 75 per cent of the royalties or fees that might come from the areas where these minerals are discovered. Why was Premier Regan so happy? Why was he laughing and chuckling so much ? He has an election coming up this year and has to try and make it sound like it really amounts to something. What will it be 75 per cent of? It will be 75 per cent of what the federal government decides it is going to be. Those three provinces will have no control over the administration, no control over the pace of development, no control over whether they go with companies that put their facilities on shore or not, or whether they have to employ Nova Scotians, New Bruns-wickers or Prince Edward Islanders. That will all be left to the minister and his government.
Would any one laugh and say this is a tremendous monument to confederation, if he did not have an ulterior purpose? There is only one reason-the election. Premier Regan should be cfying all the way to the legislative assembly because of what he had to accept from the federal Liberals.
In addition, it has not yet been revealed-and it may be changed as I am revealing it-that the federal government is insisting that these three provinces cannot impose any provin-
February 23, 1977

cial corporation or any provincial taxes on the income of permit holders in this offshore region. They are allowed to get 75 per cent of the royalties and fees, whatever they may be and whenever they come in, but they are not allowed to impose any other provincial tax on the income of the permit holders. That is some deal!
They have the maritime offshore resources board with three members from the three provinces and three from the federal government. If any decisions cannot be agreed to, or if there is a tie in any particular respect, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is the final authority. It is a complete sell-out, an admission that the federal government has complete control. That is not acceptable in Newfoundland; it is not acceptable in Quebec. It is not acceptable to the Progressive Conservative party of Canada which has a policy entirely contrary to the one being administered by this government. This is a party that believes in a federal system. It believes in having strong regions and strong provinces as well as a strong federal government.
This party has made it clear that when it takes power the PC government is going to recognize the offshore provinces as having ownership and control of the minerals that lie off their shores on the continental shelf. It will give them some kind of a future. We all know that when the money comes in, if it ever comes in, eventually it will reduce the equalization payment and the need for it. But that is not the only reason. These provinces want to control the rate of the development. They want to see their own citizens share in it. They want to see that the oil companies build onshore in their province if they are using their resource offshore, and for a variety of other reasons. That is enough, I believe, to ensure our support in British Columbia and all four of the Atlantic provinces when the next election comes.
At the time publicity was given to this agreement between the maritime provinces and Canada, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources indulged in a bit of bullying. He decided that he would bully the province of Newfoundland while this agreement was being announced and he made a statement that EastCan had been talking to him and told him they were not prepared to go ahead with an exploration program next summer unless a dispute between them and the Newfoundland government over oil and gas regulations proposed by the Newfoundland government was settled. Now the Newfoundland government has prepared its own regulations and regime for the offshore, just as the federal government did a year ago. We have not seen the federal government's regulations since. They were promised last year but the regulations and the legislation are still not here. Well, Newfoundland is doing the same. It is giving the oil companies its suggested oil and gas regulations for their comments. So the minister made the statement that EastCan was not going to explore or drill next year because of these regulations which Newfoundland proposed and because of the jurisdictional dispute. This was an attempt to bluff the province of Newfoundland into surrendering on the offshore minerals question.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP FAIR AND JUST POLICIES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's dwindling supplies of oil and natural gas pose serious problems for the people of this country. It is therefore fit and proper that the government's policies for dealing with these problems should be discussed and, where necessary, criticized. Since I have only 20 minutes at my disposal I am prevented from dealing with the wide range of issues involved. I will therefore confine myself to dealing with two apsects of the energy situation.
The first matter I want to deal with is the government's failure to ensure that the increased prices being charged Canadian consumers are in fact used for the purpose of discovering and developing new supplies of oil and natural gas. In the past four years the price of gas has doubled and the price of crude oil has increased three-fold. The petroleum industry and the government have consistently maintained that
[Mr. Crosbie.)
these increases in price are necessary to ensure the cash flow needed to stimulate exploration and development. What has been the result? Exploration has not kept pace with the increased prices consumers have been required to pay. As a matter of fact, in 1975 there was a decline in exploration activity which represented the pressure on the government by the oil companies to raise prices. We are seeing a continuous decline in exploration.
At page 36 of the study "An Energy Strategy for Canada" we find that for every $1 increase in the price of a barrel of oil the industry will get 25 cents per barrel even if there is no increased exploration. If the companies carry out sufficient exploration work they will get 56 cents out of each $1 of the price increase. The federal government will get nothing; the balance will go to the producing provinces. On page 38 of the energy strategy study we find this illuminating statement:
Current estimates suggest that with existing fiscal systems and prices that gradually increase towards current international levels, the industry will retain, after taxes and royalties, in excess of $3 billion per year (in 1975 dollars) on the average, over the next five years.
If ever there was a windfall, this is it. The government has repeatedly assured the House that it would monitor these windfall revenues paid to the oil industry by the consumers of this country so as to ensure that these moneys were used for exploration and development. There is no evidence that this has been done. Indeed, all the evidence indicates the contrary. The government has consistently over the years refused to follow the course advocated by the New Democratic Party, namely, that all the additional revenue from the rise in oil prices, except that part which goes to the producing provinces, should be retained by the federal government in trust for reinvestment in exploration and development. This money could be paid to the industry as exploration programs are carried out, or the money could be utilized by Petro-Canada to carry on exploration offshore and for the development of our heavy oil and the oil sands in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
The second matter that I wish to deal with in the short time at my disposal concerns the efforts being made to push the construction of a Mackenzie Valley pipeline as a solution to Canada's need for natural gas supplies. It seems to me that this is an appropriate time for the House to express its opinion on this matter and at the conclusion of my remarks I propose to move an amendment which will give the House an opportunity to do so. It seems to me it is further made necessary by a statement which appears in this afternoon's papers from Washington where discussions are being held between the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) and the President of the United States. In passing, Mr. Speaker, I want to pay tribute to the Prime Minister. I am sure all of us were proud of the eloquent and timely speech that he made to the Congress of the United States in which he represented the views, I believe, of the great majority of the people of Canada. The report from Washington reads as follows:
A Canadian official indicated here Tuesday that Prime Minister Trudeau is ready to do all he can to speed a decision on construction of the multimillion
February 23, 1977

dollar Mackenzie Valley pipeline to carry Alaskan gas to Americans ... the official said Trudeau explained to Carter that he would "like to be in a position not to embarrass him over the pipeline".
To me, Mr. Speaker, that has a very ominous ring and I think we ought to face up at this time to this question of the construction of a Mackenzie Valley pipeline. Let us recognize, in the first place, that the primary purpose of this pipeline is to move Prudhoe Bay gas from Alaska to the United States. We should recognize that the benefits to Canada are minimal. The best estimates of our proven gas reserves in the Mackenzie Valley are somewhere between four trillion cubic feet and five trillion cubic feet. May 1 point out that already all but 1.4 trillion cubic feet of that gas has been contracted to gas companies in the United States. But even if we get all the gas in the Delta-and there is every reason to believe we will not-five trillion cubic feet is only the equivalent of what we export to the United States over a five-year period.
It is a travesty to suggest that we should build pipeline at a cost of $8 billion-though the cost is much more likely to be $10 billion or $12 billion-and at the same time suffer the economic and monetary dislocations of such high capital expenditures, as well as environmental damage and a disturbing impact on our native people, in order to get a quantity of gas which we could procure by a more intensive exploration program in the southern areas of Canada and by offshore drilling.
There is nothing which calls into question more the viability of this proposed pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley than the fact that Canadian Arctic Gas Pipe Line Company has stated publicly that it will require financial guarantees from the Canadian government. One might well ask why, if this is a viable project, and since it is primarily going to carry Alaskan gas to the United States, the Canadian government should be asked to give financial guarantees.
As a matter of fact, I think it is significant that, despite repeated public statements to the effect that they want financial guarantees, this company has never formally applied for those guarantees. Why? Because they are waiting for a favourable report from the National Energy Board. Once they have a conditional permit in their hot little hands they are counting on pressure from Washington to secure financial guarantees from the government of Canada. The government of Canada will then be in the very difficult position of having either to refuse these guarantees or having to set aside a recommendation of the National Energy Board. The government will further be in the awkward position that, if the Prime Minister of Canada has agreed with the President of the United States to speed up a decision on the matter, and if the United States President has already indicated to Congress his preference for the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, they will have no alternative but to grant those guarantees and allow construction of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline.
The Canadian Arctic Gas Pipe Line Company Limited would then be able to say to the Canadian government, "You knew all along that we would need financial guarantees before we could proceed with this project, and you allowed the National Energy Board to grant us a permit to build the
Energy Policy
Mackenzie Valley pipeline; therefore, automatically, the granting of the permit involves financial guarantees". Financial guarantees for what? For moving 35 trillion cubic feet of gas from Prudhoe Bay to the United States? In the process Canada will get all the financial dislocation, all the environmental damage, all the dislocation of our native people, to secure, at most, five trillion cubic feet of gas; and the prospects are that most of that gas will go to the United States.
It will go to the United States first of all because, as 1 already said, most of it is contracted to American gas companies, but, secondly because that gas will come onstream ahead of the Prudhoe Bay gas and consequently it will come at a time when we will not be in great need of natural gas; and under the National Energy Board Act, which says that surplus gas can be exported to the United States, the American companies of course will apply for permission to export the gas from the Mackenzie Delta to the United States. It should be kept in mind that in this country we have, it is estimated, nearly 60 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. Annually we consume 1.5 trillion cubic feet and we export to the United States 1 trillion cubic feet. That means that we have quite a few years of lead time to find new sources of gas to meet Canadian needs without the environmental damage and the creation of problems for our native people that are associated with this project.
We maintain that the Mackenzie Valley pipeline is not needed at this time, that it has no economic benefit for Canadians. Naturally, we sympathize with our American neighbours about their desire to get Alaskan gas shipped from Prudhoe Bay to the United States, but I submit that there is a much less expensive and much less damaging alternative which should be considered. Proposals have been put forward by which we could ship gas from Prudhoe Bay down along the Alaska Highway which would provide the Americans with a land bridge that would take their gas directly to the United States. That should be considered if three conditions are met: first of all, that the Americans finance the pipeline; second, that the Americans be prepared to accept the one trillion cubic feet of export commitments which we have, and meet those commitments out of Prudhoe Bay gas. That would save Canada one trillion cubic feet of gas per year. In five years we would get all the gas which we would get from building the Mackenzie Valley pipeline.

The third condition I would impose would be that during the construction of that pipeline, if it is approved, every cubic foot of gas which we continue to export to the United States should be on a swap basis, so that when their line is in operation we would recover that gas from the line going to the United States and we would have at that time six trillion or seven trillion cubic feet of gas coming to us which we could take when we wanted it and as we wanted it.

February 23, 1977
Energy Policy
It seems to me that if those three conditions were met we should give serious consideration to what is commonly called the Alcan route, although I think the direction would be different from what has been proposed. But the general idea is to take the pipeline down along the Alaska Highway where there would be less environmental damage, less dislocation of the native people, and where we would not be required to make the tremendous capital investment which we will need for oil sand development, perhaps for nuclear reactors and for other forms of energy which this country must have.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) has said, as does this study, an "Energy Strategy for Canada", that we will need, between now and 1990, $ 180 billion in capital expenditures to meet our energy requirements. I contend that if this country ties up anywhere from $8 billion to $12 billion in a pipeline that will give us minimal benefits, we will not have the capital to develop the other resources which we must have in the 1980s and 1990s to keep the Canadian people from freezing in the dark.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP FAIR AND JUST POLICIES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS RESOURCES

Therefore, I hope that the House will avail itself of this opportunity to express to the government how we feel about the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, and I suggest that we should do it now, not if we wait until the National Energy Board has made its report and the cabinet has made its report. The reports will not be referred to the House of Commons, as the ministers have said repeatedly. This is the time, now, before they have gone too far, before the Prime Minister has made too many commitments, before the government has laid all its plans on the basis of a pipeline which will bring only minimal benefits to Canada, for this House to say in clear and certain terms that we think this project is not in the best interests of the Canadian people.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and this House expresses its opinion that the proposed construction of a Mackenzie Valley pipeline is not in the best interests of the Canadian people.

Let me make it quite clear that the plan for insulation and conservation offered to the provinces of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia was to deal with two specific questions and needs. Hon. members will recall that the Premier of Nova Scotia appealed for assistance because electrical energy rates in his province had gone up very substantially and were likely to go up very much more in the near future. He said his province had nearly the highest electrical energy rate in the country. The highest, of course, is Prince Edward Island. When we looked at the situation it was quite clear there was a unique need in these two provinces. Prince Edward Island depended for 100 per cent of its electrical energy on oil; they had no hydro capacity. In the case of Nova Scotia, roughly two-thirds of all electrical energy was generated from oil.
The stated policy of this government which was put forward to parliament in the document "An Energy Strategy for Canada"-Policies for Self-Reliance" was to reduce our dependence on foreign oil. That was the goal. Clearly, there was a question of national interest on the problem that these two provinces had to deal with-their heavy dependence on foreign oil. When we looked at the situation it seemed to us that the most appropriate way of providing assistance to Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island was to do it in a way which would be fully consistent with the strategy of reducing our dependence on foreign oil. If we had accepted the proposal of the Premier of Nova Scotia to provide subsidies, we would have been going counter to that particular objective for Canada because we would have been subsidizing the continuation of the greater use of oil indirectly. The proposal we put forward for insulation in a typical home will provide savings in one year greater that the additional cost of electrical power for one year. Not only is it an advantage on a one-year basis, but it is a permanent advantage to home owners in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. The saving continues from year to year, whereas any other kind of assistance, such as a subsidy,
February 23, 1977

would be temporary. We also provided incentives and assistance with respect to conservation measures for industry, and also substitution arrangements in the province of Nova Scotia for the conversion of an oil-fired generating facility to a coal-fired one.
I think it is clear that this is a unique situation. It is not discriminatory in the sense that other provinces would qualify because the next nearest province, when it comes to the question of electrical energy generated from oil, has about half the .dependence of Nova Scotia. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) had some figures and I should like to reply to them. Newfoundland, fortunately, is very little dependent upon foreign oil for the generation of electricity on the island and in Labrador. The figures I have been given for electrical generation for 1976-and these exclude the demand for exports to Quebec-are 7,800 gigawatt hours and for oil-generated electricity in all of Labrador and Newfoundland are 400 gigawatt hours. The oil-fired generation compared to the total generation used in the province of Newfoundland is, therefore, in the order of 5 per cent, very much lower than that for Nova Scotia which has close to 66 per cent.
I can understand that the hon. member for St. John's West would want to emphasize the hydro potential for Newfoundland. He knows I share his interest in seeing that development take place. Indeed, I met with him a little under a year ago when he was minister of energy in the province of Newfoundland to discuss precisely that question and to try to see what steps the federal government could take to bring about the realization of the Gull Island facility.
I answered a question in the House today from one of the hon. member's colleagues. I said I had been in touch with the Premier of Newfoundland to raise with him the question of the transmission assistance which we had offered. There is $343 million still on the table with respect to the transmission of power from Gull Island to Newfoundland. I offered to discuss with him, as well, other forms of arrangement which the federal government might enter into. This would be a new departure, possibly even involving equity on the part of the federal government, which would deal with the generation facilities at Gull Island. I asked the premier, if he was still interested in pursuing this matter, and if so, to designate a senior official so that we could get on with the job of identifying the costs and engineering needed to bring about this major facility.
As hon. members will understand, the announcement two weeks ago of the establishment of a maritime energy corporation is very much a part of what I see to be the over-all strategy for the Atlantic provinces. I would expect there might be as much as 1,000 megawatts of surplus power in the Gull Island facility. I realize that the maritime provinces are going to require power in the future. Some of that additional power might well come from Gull Island. The maritime energy corporation would be the logical institution to purchase that power, to decide how it would be used and to arrange, if necessary, during certain periods of the year or perhaps certain hours of the day the sale of any of that power which might be
Energy Policy
surplus to the maritime region. I do not mean to suggest that I see the Gull Island facility as the sole answer to the future needs of the maritime region. Clearly, other projects are going to be important. It may be that an additional nuclear facility in New Brunswick should be contemplated very soon. I hope we will receive sufficiently encouraging news with respect to the study being taken on the Fundy tides. The project has been long discussed and the potential of it has been long recognized, but until very fairly recently the economics of it have not been very encouraging. These are some of the points I would make to the hon. member with regard to the maritimes.
The last point I want to deal with is the one the hon. member raised with regard to the offshore resources of Canada and the ownership of them. I can understand why he would want to take a strong, perhaps even aggressive stance on this. To some extent he has been the architect of a situation which is developing in Newfoundland, one about which I have very serious concerns. I think that when Canadians in other parts of the country know the facts they will have concern as well. I refer, of course, to the whole question of exploration and drilling on the north shore of Labrador.
The hon. member for St. John's West was a former minister of energy of the province of Newfoundland. It is he who can accept the credit and, presumably, the responsibility for having designed the new set of regulations which have in confidence been presented to the exploration consortium. That consortium has reacted in a positive way, positive at least in the sense of saying that the regulations presented to them are unacceptable, they are too stringent. They are far more stringent than the new set of principles which has been tabled by the federal government with respect to oil and gas regulations. They have indicated that if the Newfoundland government is prepared to give undertakings that their regulations, in the event that they were to win a court case with respect to offshore resources, will be no more onerous than those which the federal government has already put on the table, they would be prepared to go ahead. I can understand why the hon. member would want to take an aggressive stance on this. He perhaps, more than any other man, is the architect of the confrontation which has developed between the consortium and the province of Newfoundland.
Let us be quite clear about what is involved here. I have said that I might want to use some moral suasion to put before the Newfoundland government a very good argument to alter their position in light of the facts. The hon. member is suggesting that the federal government is in some way trying to steal the resources which rightfully belong to Newfoundland. He does not realize that as a result of his action he is preventing the people of Newfoundland from benefiting from the potential development of those resources. Close to $100 million of exploration activity was slated for the east shore this year. About one half of that was in Labrador. Unless we can find some accommodation between this consortium and the Newfoundland government, between $50 million and $60 million in exploration activity will not take place this coming season.

February 23, 1977

That clearly rests on the shoulders of the hon. member as much as anybody else.
The major part of the remaining portion will be undertaken by Petro-Canada. The Conservative party have been very ambivalent, and that is putting it charitably, about Petro-Canada. Their leader has said that he would wind down or wind up-it is never quite clear-Petro-Canada. He has never said how he would have dealt with the problem of offshore exploration in the maritimes if it had not been for Petro-Canada. The activity of Petro-Canada is essential to the maritime region at the present time. It may well become increasingly important to the Labrador offshore as well.
It is probably hoping too much that we will hear from opposition spokesmen today what they would propose by way of changes in the strategy which the government of Canada has adopted. I hope they will show interest before the standing committee which deals with this important matter. I hope we will hear from members opposite what they think the pricing policy should be with respect to energy. I hope we will hear from them with respect to Canadian content. We have not heard anything from them with respect to Canadian content.
I hope we will hear from members opposite as to our obligations under the International Energy Agency and the sharing obligations which Canada has accepted under our obligations to that international agency. 1 hope they will have something to say about the targets for conservation. I hope they will address themselves to some of the major national issues. I know that we can again look forward to some glowing constituency speeches in the future, but I hope they will deal with national issues as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased on this day allotted the opposition to take part in a debate on a topic of interest to all Canadians, namely the energy problem in Canada.
1 shall waste no time in dealing with the scandals that beset the recent sale of Canadian reactors to foreign countries. I would rather take advantage of this debate to point out the growing enslavement of humankind at the hands of international or multinational monopolies exercised over every form of energy.
However, Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell my hon. colleagues that I recently met a businessman from Ontario who was proud of his car, a 1973 Buick burning only one gallon of gas to run 62 miles. That man also had another Buick, a 1976, that runs only 14 miles per gallon of gas. The difference between the two lies in the fact-and this I saw myself-that the 1973 Buick was scientifically and mechanically improved by his son, an engineer, who also made similar adjustments on seven or eight other cars belonging to his friends. Because his son was an engineer, extremely competent and specialized in mechanics, it seems he had discovered the secret of considerable saving of gas. However, Mr. Speaker, that engineer died in an automobile accident; his car smashed into a tree under as yet undetermined circumstances. That learned engineer, Mr. Speaker, whose father is still living, had never accepted any of the offers made to him for his secret.
Mr. Speaker, we have been brainwashed into thinking there is a shortage of energy in Canada so that we could be better exploited through increasing prices; while prices go up regularly, the product is still at the disposal of consumers who are fleeced through ever higher prices. Mr. Speaker, how can the governments seriously want to reduce the consumption of energy when, for instance, on gas alone, both at the federal and provincial levels, they reap in taxes more that 60 per cent of the retail price?
How can the governments be interested in reducing gas consumption for the benefit of consumers when they are the very first beneficiaries of the various taxes on gas?
Just as governments exploit consumers through various taxes on energy, so do the Arab countries in turn bleed the energy consuming countries. The lack of foresight of governments towards energy, particularly since the last 30 years when there was no forecast as to eventual energy needs, makes it that much easier for the Arab countries to exploit the energy situation in the world. The energy shortage is not caused by a limited potential for energy resources, but by a lack of long term planning in the development of energy resources.
February 23, 1977

Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, natural resources planning, like energy resources, has been left so far in the hands of multinationals with the sole purpose, which is not the public weal, of making profits at the risk of causing the death of people in years to come.
Mr. Speaker we have squandered our resources in raw materials through exploitation and exportation to enhance our balance of payments position without any consideration for our power supply and future needs.
Mr. Speaker, Algeria keeps its power resources in gas and oil for its citizens. Future needs in that area have priority over immediate gains for multinationals. Algerians are not afraid they might be short of power tomorrow morning. They are not concerned about the interests of international traffickers and owners of multinationals operating in that field. It is scandalous, Mr. Speaker, to realize that $125 million a day-I repeat, $125 million "a day"-are taken out of the pockets of western world residents to go into the coffers of Arab countries. This money is generated only through price increases of petroleum products decreed by the Oil Producing and Exportating Countries which they control; $125 million in benefits are gathered every day after the various increases which have occurred in the last five years. This Arab money goes into Swiss banks which in turn invest it for them throughout the world, even in Canada. The Arabs have already started to buy oil products with our own money through Swiss banks.
Mr. Speaker, the same racket is building up in the field of nuclear energy. International financiers who control world monopolies have started to do with nuclear energy what the Arabs do with oil. International finance magnates are against solar energy because they have yet to gain exclusive control over the sun. Therefore they favour nuclear energy which is easily controlled.
Mr. Speaker, the sun existed before multinational companies. It has never disappointed us. The sun was there before finance companies; God created the sun to serve man, to warm him. Tycoons have not yet bought the sun to control it, sell it or treat it as they see fit. Nuclear energy companies-and I could name many of them-are paying scientists to try to have us believe that solar energy is impractical, uneconomic, and so on.
The magazine Science Forum for August 1976, page 17, reports that, according to a release published on March 3, 1976 by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Canadian federal government spent $84.8 million for nuclear research during fiscal year 1975-76. The government spent $10.5 million for research on oil and gasoline, $8.6 million for energy conservation, $4.9 million for transport and transmission, and $2.8 million for coal energy.
The federal government has spent $1.6 million to assist research on solar and geothermic energy; so they spent 75 times more money on nuclear than on solar research. These figures speak for themselves, Mr. Speaker. The government does not want any research on solar energy; they want to develop nuclear energy because the international financial
Energy Policy
trusts are for research on nuclear energy whereas scientists are in favour of solar energy.
Mr. Speaker, in the April 28, 1976 issue of La Presse we could read that Mr. Claude Leroy, 29, who has a degree in optics, has discovered a revolutionary process for the use of solar energy at low cost.
Mr. Leroy has developed a solar collector into which the solar rays penetrate in concentrated form thanks to a captor, and they cannot go out of this collector any more.
In the February 20, 1977 issue of the Ottawa paper Le Droit, another scientist says the following: According to Mr. Jean-Yves Cousteau, the sun could provide 80 per cent of the energy needed in the year 2000.
He feels that solar energy is the only solution . . . The main source of solar energy is found in the oceans. Two thirds of all the solar energy which reaches the earth fall into the oceans . . . Properly tapped, solar energy could easily represent four fifths of the world energy before the year 2000 . . . Moreover, nuclear energy is the greatest danger . . . for its is a non solution . . . According to the data published by the United Nations, the $850 million which will be spent on nuclear energy up to the year 2000 will meet the needs of only 20 per cent of the world demand.
Mr. Speaker, a very interesting report appeared on January 15, 1977, again in La Presse, in which Jean-Pierre Bonhomme, the author, states:
Solar heat will liberate the Quebec household.
And again in La Presse, on April 24:
Solar Energy Electricity will come from the cosmos.
The newspaper adds that engineer Peter E. Glaser of the Arthur D. Little Company of Cambridge, Massachussets, suggests the installation of an orbital power station that would use ...
. . . huge surfaces of solar collectors to transform sun light directly into electricity in the same way as solar mirrors are used to feed energy to most of present day spatial devices.
Mr. Speaker, in Le Devoir of April 22, 1976, Ottawa architect Michael Glover contends .. .
. . . that direct loans at low interest rates or tax reductions should be allowed to citizens who install home heating systems fed by solar energy.
Also, in the Canadian Consumer magazine of June I, 1976, page 33, Mr. Ron Argue had this to say:
Solar energy heating is the solution to traditional heating systems.
Again in Le Devoir of December 31, 1976, in an article signed by Mr. Gilles Provost:
Solar heating can compete with electricity.
For the first time, an American study states that solar energy heating can compete with electric heating.
Mr. Speaker, Ralph Nader who is well known in the United States stated the following:
If the sun belonged to Exxon, we would already be using solar energy.
Some inexhaustible, renewable, clean and free sources of energy have always been available to mankind, but science does not enable us to use them effectively. There are many scientists, handymen and even engineers who have devised techniques enabling us to take advantage of our natural wealth

February 23, 1977
Energy Policy
without destroying it, to use the revenue without depleting the capital.
Mr. Speaker, if the economic structures are inconsistent with the use of soft techniques, the conservation of resources and the biological requirements of survival, we must then alter the economy, because we cannot change the laws of physics nor those of life.
On page 52 of the same magazine I mentioned a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, we can read this, and I quote:
The choice is therefore not only political, but also social and moral. It involves much more than capital. In fact, the whole western civilization is involved in that choice.
Here is what Professor Lebreton of the University of Lyons has to say on that subject:
One has to understand what the Carnot cycle is to realize that, far from being the miraculous source of energy which we were promised, the nuclear power station opens the era of the biggest thermo-dynamic waste ever invented by man.
As for burial sites of solid and liquid wastes of high and medium radioactivity, our children will not be able either to reconvert them to potato fields. Our generation is leading its children toward the point of no return.
Mr. Pierre Dansereau said, in "La terre des hommes et le paysage interieur", and I quote:
Wisdom has more weight than science if we are to change the course leading our species to suicide.
Mr. Mouammar Kadhafi from Lybia, a world renown scientist, said:
Great and rich powers spend fabulous sums of money to make atom bombs, to develop intercontinental missiles, to implement space programs and to develop propaganda and psychological warfare plans, while the people of our planet are facing illness, hunger and skyrocketing prices. Those countries are in effect guided by the devil, and their volume of the sacred law is Malthus and not the Bible.
The great Einstein had this to say:
The scientist is aware that the applications of his research has concentrated in the hands of a small minority, first the economic, then the political power that controls the mass of the people who seem to be ever more amorphous ... He degrades himself to the point of enormously developing on orders the facilities for total destruction of mankind.
Mr. Speaker, there is not the shadow of a doubt about the form of energy Canada should have chosen to meet our future needs, those of 2000 A.D.
All scientists who worked in that field are awed at the dangers of nuclear power for the Canadian people and the people of the world. On the other hand, there is no major obstacle barring the development of solar energy in the world.
One thing specially is to be regretted. The Canadian government is selling the false advantages of nuclear energy and its CANDU reactors. World uranium reserves on which CANDU are based are 85 per cent controlled by four world powers: the United States, Canada, South Africa and Australia. All those countries favour nuclear energy through the mining and exporting of products used to generate nuclear energy. Those countries have a colonial approach to the Third World.
These special goods which are bringing an excellent return to the industry are armaments. In a way the energy policy has the same function as the armament policy, namely to ensure a
[Mr. Rondeau.)
steady flow of capital, to make profits, to maintain and increase domination over others.
It is more and more evident that the big concerns controlled by the state and by the private sector will try to impose on dominated countries nuclear reactors which will bring them more profits, whatever the real needs of these countries may be. The sale by Canada of a $700 million reactor to South Korea illustrates very well. Mr. Speaker, that such a contract will be of no advantage whatsoever either to the Koreans or to the Canadians, but will profit the manufacturer of this enormous hot water kettle. The colonial approach of Canada, already seen in Brazil and the West Indies, is even more patent when Canada sells CANDU reactors to countries of the third world.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote a paragraph from a book about nuclear energy by Fred H. Knelman, called Nuclear Energy. Here is what he said, on page 238:

I regret that I cannot support the amendment as proposed at this time, because we do not have the important benefit of the findings of the Berger commission and of the National Energy Board. To take a position now would be premature, in my opinion, and would preclude consideration of a most impor-tantr set of facts. Indeed, it could be interpreted as an affront to the Berger commission and to the National Energy Board.
Canada is fortunate in the variety and size of such undeveloped energy sources as the Alberta tar sands, the
February 23, 1977

western Canadian coal fields, the Ontario uranium deposits, the hydroelectric capacity of Quebec and Labrador, tidal power in the Bay of Fundy and the immense renewable energy source inherent in our forests. The challenge is to produce and utilize these sources so as to decrease our present dependence on dwindling oil and gas reserves, and to do it in ways that provide the greatest benefits in accordance with economic, social and environmental consideration.
Time is a basic problem. It takes time to build a hydro-electric dam. It takes time to develop a new coal deposit. It takes time to construct a nuclear reactor. It takes time to create tidal power development. And last but not least, it takes time to accumulate the capital for the type of large-scale enterprise which is necessary to ameliorate our heavy dependence on offshore oil-and this time is not measured in years but in decades. Thus, it is a venture for many years to come. We must learn to live with the fact that for the next 10 to 15 years Atlantic Canada will continue to import over 100 million barrels of oil per year to sustain an energy system greatly dependent on this commodity.
Dramatic increases in the cost of electric power in areas of Atlantic Canada have placed the region at a competitive disadvantage in the expansion of its industrial and manufacturing sector and inflicted a great measure of hardship on large segments of the population. While I intend to propose some suggestions to reduce these disadvantages, it must be recognized that this will be a battle not quickly or easily won. In the short term, until a fundamental improvement in the situation can be achieved there is a broad scope for cost-sharing programs and federal grants to promote energy efficiencies in new and existing operations. In the long term-beyond 1990-the prospects look far better as long as programs to exploit other energy sources are begun now. It is in the short term where our most intractable problems lie. Consequently, we must distinguish between short run policy initiatives, which will necessarily be of a palliative nature, and long run policy initiatives with which more fundamental changes in the energy system will be achieved. With this is mind, the objectives we are aiming at can be itemized.
I am going to mention a few of the objectives I would like to see us explore. First, diversify the energy base in Atlantic Canada, thereby reducing that region's overwhelming dependence on offshore oil. Second, pool wherever possible the various energy systems in Atlantic Canada to achieve economic and technical efficiencies of scale, and in conjunction with this strategy strengthen energy interconnections with adjacent provinces and states. Third, to introduce renewable energy forms to the greatest extent feasible, even if these forms have to be initially subsidized. Fourth, to reduce the rate of increase in future energy costs. Fifth, to achieve a much higher level of co-operation among the governments involved. Sixth, to reduce the energy demand so that pressures on supply are eased. Seventh, to set up an effective program of public education to ensure support and understanding of the initiatives being taken.
Energy Policy
In my opinion the government has not acted to diversify the energy base in Atlantic Canada and thus reduce the region's overwhelming dependence on offshore oil. While it has introduced an ad hoc program to insulate older homes in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, which should enable the owners of these homes to use less electricity, it has in fact, done nothing to reduce the cost of electric energy or the region's dependence on offshore oil which is increasing in price. A real conservation program would do more than insulate older homes. A government really interested in conservation would have regional and branch offices in the Atlantic provinces and a program that would reduce energy waste in commercial and industrial undertakings. It would work with DREE to promote greater energy efficiency and work with the provinces to develop a comprehensive conservation program. Perhaps its first move would be to extend its present band-aid approach at least to all the Atlantic provinces.
Clearly, the power pool concept achieving economic and technical efficiencies of scale is a major step in the direction of lower power cost. While the maritime provinces have taken a giant step in this direction with the proposed maritim'e power corporation, the federal government, which dragged its feet for years on the Fundy tidal power study, has adopted a different pose. Instead of offering to take an equity position and financially support such a worthy concept, the government is sitting on its hands. The government seems to lack an over-all strategy in approaching the problems of Atlantic Canada. It has announced financing for studies of some renewable energy forms which are quite commendable. But what about other energy forms, and what about indigenous energy sources in Atlantic Canada? There is no over-all strategy. The government cannot, or will not, come to grips with the total problem and in concert with the Atlantic provinces develop a strategy designed to solve the problems. As 1 have indicated, there are no easy answers, but there should be a commitment and a dedication on the part of the federal government to finding the answers.
I have some initiatives that I feel the government should immediately undertake in order to deal more effectively with the electric energy problems in Atlantic Canada. First, I believe the government should co-operate with the governments of the Atlantic provinces in giving priority to the economic supply and distribution of electrical energy in the region. The areas of co-operation I contemplate would include the development of a full maritime power pool with strong interconnections with adjacent areas of Canada and the United States in order that all the benefits of power pool operations may be optimized. This, in my view, would be a major step in the direction of integrating other provinces and other power pools into an eventual national power grid. Second, the government of Canada should give financial support to the Atlantic provinces to enhance the construction of electrical and transmission facilities which would be part of an agreed master plan of electrical energy supply. The agreed master plan to which I refer should not be dictated by Ottawa but should be the result of leadership given by Ottawa and

February 23, 1977
Energy Policy
co-operative action with the provinces. The provinces have demonstrated their ability to reach accord in matters of this kind. Ottawa has not demonstrated its commitment to the same extent.
Third, Canada should encourage the study and development of unused hydroelectric sites-especially the large, remote sites in northern areas of Canada-which could supply renewable energy into a Canadian electrical energy distribution system. The untapped hydro resources of 20 rivers in Labrador, the most dramatic being the Gull Island and Muskrat Falls sites, are the most attractive untapped hydroelectric sites in America.
Fourth, the government should accelerate studies of the feasibility of tidal power generation and encourage development of those sites which show a beneficial energy supply to Canadian energy requirements. Since 1969, lack of foresight and the complete absence of government policy have seen these studies move forward at a snail's pace. Even considering this continent's energy needs in the 1990s, and projecting the dwindling supplies and increasing prices of fossil fuels, Fundy looms as an attractive opportunity with tremendous socioeconomic benefits for all of eastern Canada.
Fifth, the government should investigate the use of low grade wood fibre as an important energy source in conjunction with an improved forest management program. Incentives should be considered to encourage wood-using industries to become self-sufficient for energy from wood fibre such as bark and debris from harvest. The government of Canada should make funds available to the eastern provinces to fund a study to determine the wood energy capability and uses of the wood resources in these provinces and a pilot project should be initiated to explore the utilization of waste wood in energy production.
Sixth, Canada should encourage research and development in all fields related to energy conservation from renewable and indigenous sources. We should challenge the free enterprise system with tax incentives and grants to move into this field and, without limiting the scope or generality of my suggestion,
I would be particularly interested in seeing the private sector of our economy tackle the problem of generating electrical energy and heat from the sun, paying particular attention to storage problems, the efficiency of solar cells and establishing Canadian pre-eminence in a major energy source for the future.
Seventh, we should greatly accelerate programs leading to energy conservation and provide incentives to encourage the correction of sources of energy waste. Eighth, we should encourage the use of deposits of low quality coal and peat in eastern Canada as fuel for the generation of electrical energy. Ninth, we should encourage research and development into the feasibility of using new energy sources such as solar, wind, waves and biomass.
Finally, the government so far has failed to meet the challenge of a long-term solution to the energy problems of

Atlantic Canada. The government has instituted a series of ad hoc measures, made grants for the construction of facilities, provided assistance for two provinces by way of an insulation program, and made some research grants. However, it has no master plan and it appears to lack direction, purpose and an understanding of both the potential and the problems in the Atlantic provinces. 1 have great respect for the minister and his senior officials, and I hope they will pay careful attention to the suggestions and recommendations 1 have made and that the energy department will demonstrate some energy in acting quickly on them. 1 can sum up my remarks in three words: Give leadership, please.

Under the federalism of the present Canadian government, Mr. Speaker-and I pay tribute today to the people of Alberta-they tried to convince the latter that they should give up a part of the surtax charged to the Americans so that all the Canadian people may benefit from a Canadian price. That is Canadian federalism, and that is what they try to sell in my province. And when I see a member of parliament like the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) make the comments which I have just heard, I am puzzled! As a matter of fact, that is what Canadian federalism is aiming at, to enable all Canadians to take advantage of the resources of some parts of the country, and this is precisely what the people of Alberta have understood and I pay tribute to them for it. They agreed then and still agree today and since I am speaking of these benefits which my fellow citizens of the province of Quebec have taken advantage of, it enabled each and every citizen of the province of Quebec to get not less than $500 since the introduction of the price compensation program. In other words, between January 1, 1974 and June 1, 1976, this brought Quebec-and I hope I am talking loud enough for the whole population of the province to hear me-this brought $2,024 billion, and that is not all.
In 1976, even though deliveries to the United States went down because of a program aiming at keeping energy in Canada, this has been worth about $800 million to the population of Quebec. It is easy enough to add this up and to see what advantages the population has had because of this oil

February 23, 1977
Energy Policy
price compensation program. This-and I say so once again for the benefit of my colleague from St. John West-this is the good federalism of the Trudeau government. It consists in making all regions of the country benefit from the wealth of other regions. Today, Alberta and Saskatchewan have the resources from which we can all benefit. Tomorrow, it might be New Brunswick, the riding of my colleague from York-Sun-bury (Mr. Howie), or another riding, maybe that of my colleague from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie). Who knows?
Mr. Speaker, because of the conservation policy and the price policy within the export program and the compensation program, the province of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces have received nearly $4 billion since 1974. I believe that this is evidence enough of the good federalism of the Trudeau government, and that there is no need to continue any further.
I would also like to speak a little of the action taken by the government to reduce the difficulties caused by the energy crisis for Canadians. First, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, through its capable minister, established an oil price policy aimed at reaching international prices as soon as possible. And this for several reasons. One, Mr. Speaker, is that Canadians must urgently become aware that oil is exhaustible and that the more quickly people will become aware of the importance of saving and keeping oil, the better and the longer we could count on the oil reserves required to heat our homes and drive our cars.
There is also a second effect which is to allow the oil companies to produce enough revenues to speed up and not only maintain exploration operations. Those who are familiar with oil companies' operations know very well that 1976 was a particularly busy year in this field in order to provide Canadians with oil at a cost they are not used to paying. If we compare the price that we Canadians pay with the price that Japanese or French or English people must pay, we see that in some country the price is almost twice the Canadian price. Once again, all Canadians benefit from this. This is another virtue of the Canadian federalism of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in the sense that some regions profit from the wealth of others.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, 1976 was an exceptional year in exploration and it is good to see that corporations have confidence in the steps taken by the Canadian government. Corporations are also aware of their responsibilities to develop supply sources that will allow Canadians and the petrochemical industry and the Canadian industry in general to get oil supplies at a price much lower that the import price.
And exploration was extended, Mr. Speaker, up to the frontier areas of the country.
Some other measures have also been taken to ensure better oil recovery. In some oil producing countries like Saudi Arabia, for instance, only 30 to 40 per cent of the known reserves in some wells are extracted. In Canada, the promotion campaign for heavy oil exportation resulted in an increase in the rate of recovery from the sands from Lloydminster and elsewhere which resulted in a very large increase in the
[Mr. Dupras.)
recovery of heavy oil and also, Mr. Speaker, a better market for heavy oil for the benefits of producers as in Canada we do not have any industry capable of using that oil, and under the campaign launched on January 1, 1977, I think that no fewer than 115,000 barrels a day are sold to the Americans.
This research is aimed at increasing the rate of recovery from traditional sources. Without new methods and expertise like the infusion of vapours and so on, this rate of recovery should reach 75 or 80 per cent in some cases. This is our goal. We are in close communication with countries in the samd situation-Venezuela, for one-which also experiences recovery problems for their oil resources.
In the replacement program for heating oil and gas, enormous amounts have been spent for research and development and this year $128 million have been spent for research. It represents a sizeable increase over past years to make Canadian experts more knowledgeable about energy production methods and not only from oil.
Seventy per cent of that amount, Mr. Speaker, is spent on nuclear research. I will come back to that later on if 1 have time.
I will deal with the steps taken by the Canadian government with regard to the creation of a Canadian petroleum company to negotiate and deal with other countries at the national level and also ensure that Canadian reserves are used in a rational way, that is that companies with additional territories will have to develop them, put them into use or give them back to the Crown so Canadian companies can develop them.
Mr. Speaker, you remember how difficult it was for some members of the opposition to accept the creation of Petro-Canada. Many countries already praise the Canadian government for its decision to create a Canadian petroleum company, so the government itself would see to the exploration and development of its natural resources that are non-renewable and that are in fact running low very fast.
Mr. Speaker, those are so many steps taken by the government to increase the viability, and in some cases, access to Canadian energy reserves.
The mover, Mr. Speaker,-
In his remarks he indicated many times that he could not find answers in the blue book entitled "An Energy Strategy for Canada . I should like to remind the hon. member that this document was written in 1976. On page 3, the second paragraph, he will read the following:
We are living in a world where past behaviour, while it provides a useful guide to future prospects, does not in itself provide sufficient information on which to base future energy policies. Energy supply projects are now so big and so expensive that one requires a much more precise recognition of the interrelationships between energy policy planning and other social and economic goals than was necessary in the past. There are a number of key questions-

There are a number of good questions that are still unanswered. One is, what will happen to international prices in the future? We all know that if it had not been for this special export tax charged to our neighbours to the south we would not have been able to adopt a Canadian price for Canadian consumers.

There is a host of steps, Mr. Speaker-unfortunately I see that you are about to tell me my time is up and recognize another member. Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the party opposite made a mistake in choosing the subject matter of its motion. It might have found another topic that could have meant a little more for the party.
