Mr. Speaker, there are a number of subjects I would like to cover in the brief time available to me. I certainly do not agree with the parliamentary secretary that we chose the wrong subject for today. We chose the right subject, with the confusion in Canada today over energy and its problems. 1 would like to touch on a few of them. Last week there was a news release by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources entitled "Role of Renewable Energy Strengthened". It states there was a $4.4 million increase for renewable energy and that a part of that was to go to biomass. I raised this subject in the Standing Committee on Natural Resources and Public Works yesterday. Neither the minister nor his officials could tell me the exact amount going to biomass because that will now be handled by the Department of Agriculture. I have been in touch with the Biomass Energy Institute. They do not know of any amount of money they are going to be receiving. Their concern is the conflict that has arisen between the Department of the Environment and the Department of Agriculture.
It does not look as though we are making any headway on biomass research. There is more confusion there. The Biomass Institute at their annual meeting last fall in Winnipeg pointed out there is very little support forthcoming from the federal government, at a time when the United States government has set up a $200 million solar energy program with biomass as one of the four components. Research into biomass and assistance to the Biomass Institute is of prime importance. There is enough biomass material going to waste every year to supply 30 times the amount humans need in the form of energy to run their civilization. That is one example why some direct action should be taken to assist biomass, rather than confusion between a couple of government departments.
1 wish to refer to a speech which the parliamentary secretary made to the Energy Conservation Conference at the University of Saskatchewan on February 18. He said:
In Sweden and Denmark and many other countries, district heating-
I imagine what he means by "district heating" is central heating, with which 1 am familiar.
Energy Policy
-usually through the co-generation of heat and electricity, is providing up to 30 per cent or more of the space heat, already in urban areas. In West Germany 28 per cent of electricity is produced from by-product steam in industry.
In Winnipeg we used to have two central heating plants. It was a very serious mistake to destroy them. They could probably be used to great advantage today.
If we were to follow these examples, we would move a long way toward our zero energy growth goal.
Unfortunately, too little consideration is being given by utilities and local governments to the role of district heating and co-generation.
Half our energy demand is for low grade heat and we should be using our waste to satisfy this demand wherever it is economically feasible.
He said that municipalities should be looking into this type of energy and district heating. What research is the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources doing into federal government complexes such as military bases? 1 will give an example. In Norfolk, Virginia, there is a large naval base which is heated by their garbage in a district heating plant. Has the minister, or have any of his officials, investigated to see if all of our military bases across Canada could be burning their garbage to provide heat? I suggest we first look at St. Jean, Quebec, where they are making many other changes. They have a heating plant that could possibly be converted. It would certainly be showing leadership if there were some research into federal government departments and military bases burning their garbage to provide heat.
The parliamentary secretary referred to the great co-operation between the oil industry and the government in producing and improving energy supplies in this country. I have received exactly the opposite information. I have been in discussion with the oil companies. All I can get from them is that excessive government regulation is devastating to the oil industry.
In recent years the degree of regulation of the Canadian petroleum industry has increased dramatically. One reason is that energy supply has come to be recognized as one of the most important determinants of our economic well being. Energy suddenly finds itself in the spotlight as the result of greatly increased prices. Canadians should be concerned that one of their major industries is subject to regulations that are often unstable, unclear and unco-ordinated to the point that the industry's performance is impaired. There is no line of communication between the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the oil companies. They go on to say:
The proposed new regulations are such that, instead of being able to plan from a fixed set of rules, the industry is in the position of having to try to predict how the ministry will use its discretion. This could turn out to be like playing blackjack in Las Vegas with the house announcing the rules as the game proceeds. Planning for major expenditures (individual wells in the Arctic can cost $25 million or more) is made very difficult when the rules are as uncertain as those set out in the proposed regulations.
The parliamentary secretary also pointed out how wonderfully Petro-Can is working. It is detrimental to Canada, causing the oil companies no end of problems. A recent story about Petro-Can states that oil firms resent the continuing loss of talent to Petro-Can. I quote:
Top petroleum executives are growing increasingly resentful about the continuing loss of middle and upper management to Petro-Canada.

February 23, 1977
Energy Policy
The heads of several companies that lost experienced people to Petro-Can during its first year of operation have taken up the matter with the federal government.
I hope there will be some line of communication there. There is no co-operation or communication. 1 he government is over regulating, telling us there is nothing to worry about and that they have a great line of communication with the oil industry. I happen to know differently. I meet with these people from time to time. 1 am very concerned about this subject. There is not a day that you pick up a newspaper that does not contain a headline such as "Oil supplies at danger level in seven years". I quote from this article:
World daily oil production rose slightly more than two per cent since 1974, and now there's a warning that if demand continues to escalate at the present rate, supplies could soon be exhausted.
I should like to know how often the minister and his officials are meeting with the drilling companies to help correct this situation. Here is another headline: "Coming oil shortage a Doomsday scenario". The text reads:
We are headed into a potentially devastating shortage of oil. Not a phoney shortage concocted by the oil companies to jack up their prices, nor a paper shortage in which, although we produce too little oil ourselves, we make up the deficit by imports, but a true, stark shortage in which we neither produce enough oil ourselves nor can buy, anywhere, the extra oil we need. If not freezing in the dark, we could be shivering in the twilight.
Yet another headline reads: "Energy shortage is possible: OECD". The article reads in part:
The organization for economic co-operation and development has called for new government policies on conservation and energy development to head off possible shortages in the mid-1980s.
The minister says he has policies. According to this article they are asking for policies. I suggest the minister should communicate with the oil industry and help the industry with its problems, not bring in more regulations. That is the last thing we need in this country today. Here is one final headline: "Taxes choking oil companies says Shell head".
C. W. Daniel, president of Shell Canada Limited, says taxes and royalties are dramatically reducing the cash flow required to enable the oil industry to expand and meet rising energy demands.
We are getting one story from the parliamentary secretary about the government's ability to communicate with the oil industry. On the other hand, this is what we read in the papers. People I know in the industry tell me that government regulations are handicapping them more and more.
